title: Shantanu and Ganga
hook: a king in heaven stares too long at the river goddess, and gods under a curse ask her for a terrible favor
carry: where the eyes go, a life follows

segments.voice: Yesterday the Adi Parva's frame closed: Astika asked, Janamejaya stopped his fire and sat down to hear the story. Did you ask plainly for what you wanted? Day seven hundred four.

A court in heaven. The gods are gathered before Brahma, and among them is a king, Mahabhisha, who earned his place there by his deeds on earth. Then the river goddess Ganga arrives. A wind lifts her garment. The gods lower their eyes. Mahabhisha doesn't. He looks, and keeps looking. Brahma sees it, and tells him: you will be born again among mortals. This part of the Kuru story starts with a stare.
screen: `A COURT IN HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS LOWER THEIR EYES.` → `ONE KING KEEPS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: This is the first piece of a new story inside the Adi Parva: Shantanu and Ganga. And the text sets it up with two curses, side by side. The first is Mahabhisha's. Brahma sends him down to be born on earth, and tells him that Ganga, the one who stole his mind, will cross him there, and that his time on earth will end when he finally loses his temper with her. Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of a good king named Pratipa. The second curse belongs to the Vasus, a group of gods. On her way back, Ganga meets them, downcast. The sage Vasishtha, they tell her, has cursed them to be born as men. They don't want to linger in human lives. So they ask Ganga a strange favor: be our mother on earth, and as each of us is born, throw us into your waters, so we're set free at once. Ganga agrees, with one condition: one son has to live, so that her time with the king isn't fruitless. The Vasus accept. Each of them gives a portion of his own power to that one son, who will live a long life on earth, and, they say, will have no children. Hold that last detail; it matters for a long time. Now go back to the fault that started it. Not a crime, not a lie: a look that wouldn't lower, in a hall where every other eye looked down. And Brahma's sentence is shaped to fit it. The one who took his mind in heaven will be the one who tries it on earth. Where Mahabhisha's attention went, his whole next life followed. And Ganga here is both the sacred river and a woman with a promise to keep.
screen: `MAHABHISHA: BORN AGAIN ON EARTH.` · `THE VASUS: CURSED BY VASISHTHA.` · `THROW US INTO YOUR WATERS.` · `ONE SON MUST LIVE.` · then, large: `WHERE THE EYES GO, A LIFE FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: A river keeps moving; it doesn't hold on. Let the breath do the same for a few rounds. Then let your eyes lower, or close, and notice where your attention wants to go: a screen, a worry, a face, a plan. Don't fight it. Just notice what keeps pulling your gaze back up. Each time you notice, let your attention come down to the breath again, the way the gods in Brahma's court lowered their eyes. The bell holds the time.
Mahabhisha. The king whose stare wouldn't lower in heaven, sent to be born on earth, where Ganga, bound by a promise to the Vasus, waits to cross him.
Your line: where the eyes go, a life follows. Today, notice one thing your eyes keep going back to, and once, on purpose, look away. Day seven hundred four.

howItsDone: At the Ganga, the river is honored as a goddess: pilgrims bathe in her waters, some carry Ganga water home in sealed vessels, and lamps are offered to her at evening aarti on her banks.

fork.setup: you're Ganga. gods cursed to be born as men beg you to be their mother and free them at birth. what do you say?
options: refuse; it's too much to ask.
agree, on condition that one son lives.
agree to all of it, no conditions.
fork.reveal: she agrees, but one son must live. each Vasu gives that son a portion of his power.

original.note: Sanskrit Gaṅgā, the river and the goddess: in this story, the mother of the Vasus on earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shantanu and Ganga is a love story.
what it means: it begins with two curses and a bargain, made before the lovers ever meet.
what a scholar hears: the Adi Parva sets Mahabhisha's curse beside the Vasus' plea before Shantanu is born.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Mahabhisha in Brahma's court; Ganga and the Vasus)

notes: All paraphrase. Check Brahma's words to Mahabhisha: that Ganga will do things displeasing to him on earth and that he will return when his anger is roused; the script says his time on earth ends 'when he finally loses his temper with her'.
Check the Vasus' bargain: Ganga's condition that one son live, each Vasu giving a portion (an eighth in the text) of his energy, and the surviving son having no offspring.
Mahabhisha 'chooses' Pratipa as his father; confirm.
howItsDone describes common Ganga practices (bathing, carrying water, evening aarti); confirm phrasing.

Editor (y3 audit): cut the 'first' claim that the Kuru story starts here (Vaishampayana's account begins earlier with genealogy); softened the Vasus' wish to the text's sense; varied the practice opener; howItsDone no longer generalizes about all Hindus.

Editor (y3 re-audit): the teach's close (we know what she promised; the story asks us to carry knowledge the characters can't), the practice (a story behind someone's actions you don't know yet) and the carry repeated the dramatic-irony angle that day 705 ('we know what he doesn't') and day 706 ('the riverbank isn't the whole story') are built on; the day now turns on its own beat, Mahabhisha's look that wouldn't lower and a sentence shaped to fit it, with a new large head, practice and carry. Day 705's review updated to match.
